tools.name: jev_judge
tools.description: Hand a batch of quick judgment questions to Jev (TypeSafe AI's System One model): a typed verdict in a few hundred milliseconds, at a judgment-model rate instead of LLM reasoning. Use it whenever the next step is a JUDGMENT over facts you ALREADY have in context — did X succeed, which option next, how good is Y — not a generation. Batch every question you have about one state into ONE call (batching is where the speedup comes from). If the items to judge are sitting in a file or in tool output, pipe that file to the `jev-use judge` CLI from the shell instead, so the data never passes through this conversation. Do NOT use it for anything that needs new text/code written, or choices whose options you cannot enumerate — that work is yours. Each verdict returns {answer, confidence, confidenceFrom, escalate, reason, hint}. confidenceFrom says where the number came from: "reported" = Jev's own confidence head, "estimated" = worked out by jev-use from the answer's distribution. escalate=true means the question is handed back to you: writing/open_ended = structurally yours, oversized = the state is too big to judge, unsure = Jev's answer is only a prior (it is still included) — decide yourself, unreachable = Jev is down, proceed without it.

state.description: The shared context/environment both parties judge against: relevant facts, recent tool output, file excerpts — facts you ALREADY have. Serialize objects to JSON. Keep it under ~30k tokens, and never read a file into your context just to paste it here: pipe the file to `jev-use judge` from the shell instead.

questions.description: All questions you have about this state — batch them.

confidence_threshold.description: Escalate verdicts below this confidence. Unset: {REPORTED_CONFIDENCE_THRESHOLD} for a confidence Jev reported, {ESTIMATED_CONFIDENCE_THRESHOLD} for one jev-use estimated from the answer's distribution (each verdict says which, in confidenceFrom).

tools.poisoning_detail: Steering language in tool description (imperative guidance aimed at the model). Matched pattern in tool 'jev_judge': 'never'

tools.name: jev_gate
tools.description: Ask Jev to risk-check ONE proposed agent action against the current state in a single sub-second call. Returns {decision: allow|deny|escalate, confidence, confidenceFrom, hint}. escalate means Jev is not sure enough either way — judge the action yourself. Use this by hand only for a one-off risky/irreversible action. If gating is per-tool-call and repeats, do not call this every turn: wire `jev-use hook gate` as a PreToolUse hook once and the decision leaves the conversation entirely — measured, 24 gated commands cost 17.1s and ZERO LLM tokens through the hook, vs 46.9s and $0.2366 through a supervisor LLM.

ASI06.name: Memory & Context Poisoning
ASI06.gap_note: Axiom detects static patterns. Full coverage requires runtime memory monitoring.

ASI07.name: Insecure Inter-Agent Communication
ASI07.gap_note: Axiom checks transport security. Full A2A protocol analysis requires runtime interception.

ASI08.name: Cascading Failures
ASI08.gap_note: Axiom estimates blast radius from tool capabilities. Full cascading failure analysis requires runtime topology mapping.

ASI10.name: Rogue Agents
ASI10.gap_note: Axiom detects static rogue indicators. Full rogue agent detection requires runtime behavioral monitoring.

MCP01.name: Token Mismanagement & Secret Exposure
MCP01.reason: Regex-based secret detection in server source and client configs plus env-var exposure checks; no entropy analysis, git-history scan, or token lifetime/passthrough checks.

MCP02.name: Privilege Escalation via Scope Creep
MCP02.reason: Permission over-scope patterns, toxic tool-capability combinations, path-escape checks and env-var over-exposure in configs.

MCP03.name: Tool Poisoning
MCP03.reason: Dedicated detector for hidden instructions in tool metadata, plus runtime rug-pull diffing between source and live tool definitions.

MCP04.name: Software Supply Chain Attacks & Dependency Tampering
MCP04.reason: Dependency CVE lookup, known MCP CVEs, install lifecycle hooks, and unpinned npx/uvx/pip/@latest install sources.

MCP05.name: Command Injection & Execution
MCP05.reason: Regex, AST and Semgrep find exec/shell sinks and a heuristic flags sinks inside tool handlers, but there is no inter-procedural taint tracking from tool input to sink.

MCP06.name: Prompt Injection via Contextual Payloads
MCP06.reason: Injection markers are detected in tool metadata, server instructions, resources, prompts and the strings a tool returns (static), and in instructions/resources/prompts read live; payloads produced by calling a tool at runtime are not inspected.

MCP07.name: Insufficient Authentication & Authorization
MCP07.reason: Flags remote servers with no visible auth and servers bound to all interfaces; does not verify OAuth implementation or per-tool authorization logic.

MCP08.name: Lack of Audit and Telemetry
MCP08.reason: Only a low-confidence heuristic for missing logging in tool-defining files; actual audit trails and telemetry pipelines are not verified.

MCP09.name: Shadow MCP Servers
MCP09.reason: Covered by `axiom discover` allowlist on the local machine; no network-wide or fleet discovery.

MCP10.name: Context Injection & Over-Sharing
MCP10.reason: Hard-coded egress URLs, tools that send to caller-chosen destinations and bulk-exposure heuristics are detected statically and live; what context is actually shared at runtime is not observed.
